en.sup: Supplied in English. The Hebrew has the adjective alone, 'a good (one)'.

01.r: A man good in character, set against the sinner.
01.n: Gesenius lists both a physical sense, good of its kind, and a moral one, 'good, kind, upright'; the moral sense fits here.

02.r: He passes on what he has, so that it reaches his grandchildren.
02.n: The verb is נָחַל, which this study renders 'inherit'; this form is causative, 'causes to inherit', as the YLT keeps it. Gesenius and BDB give the plain verb as to receive or take something as a possession. 'Leaves an inheritance' is the natural English for the causative.

03.r: With the next word, 'sons of sons': grandchildren.
03.n: BDB gives 'son', and notes that the plural can take in male and female; hence 'children's children' in most translations. The DRC rewords the phrase as 'heirs, sons, and grandsons'.

05.r: The sinner's wealth is set aside, in the end, for someone else.
05.n: A passive participle. Gesenius gives first 'to hide, to conceal', then 'to lay up, to store up'.

06.r: The one who is in the right, who ends up with the wealth.
06.n: Gesenius gives 'just, righteous'. The older translations say 'the just'.

07.n: Gesenius gives first 'strength, power, might', and then forces or an army; BDB lists 'strength, efficiency, wealth, army'. Here it is wealth, as the brief's lexicon says.

08.r: The man who goes wrong, set against the good man of the first line.
08.n: A participle, 'one who sins'. Gesenius says the verb properly means to miss, to err from the mark, as an archer does.

_extra.1: ἀνὴρ (man): added by the Greek translators, as English adds 'man'.

02.n: κληρονομέω, the verb this study renders 'inherit' in the New Testament: 'a good man will make sons of sons inherit'.

06.n: Plural in the Greek: 'for the righteous ones'.

08.n: Plural in the Greek, and a different word: ἀσεβής, 'ungodly', where the Hebrew has 'sinner'.
